content: 1. Susceptible and asymptomatic children and adults infected with HIV should be carefully monitored and managed to prevent complications. 2. To mitigate the impact of measles outbreaks, the World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of comprehensive surveillance, risk assessment, and rapid response measures, including expanded vaccination efforts. 3. Safety surveillance for potential adverse events must remain an integral part of all immunization programs. 4. WHO recommends that countries completing mass meningococcal vaccination campaigns introduce the meningococcal A conjugate vaccine into routine childhood immunization schedules within 1–5 years after the campaign, along with a one-time catch-up campaign for birth cohorts not covered by the routine program. 5. In areas where meningococcal A vaccine coverage is below 60%, periodic campaigns may be necessary to complement routine vaccination, as herd immunity may not sufficiently protect unimmunized individuals. 6. WHO advises a single-dose schedule for meningococcal A vaccine administered via deep intramuscular injection, preferably in the anterolateral thigh, between 9–18 months of age, based on local epidemiological and programmatic considerations. 7. Children who miss vaccination at the recommended age should be vaccinated as soon as possible. 8. In specific contexts where infants younger than 9 months need vaccination, a two-dose priming schedule starting at 3 months of age, with doses spaced at least 8 weeks apart, should be used. 9. MenAfriVac 5 µg is recommended for routine immunization of children aged 3–24 months, while MenAfriVac 10 µg is recommended for catch-up and periodic campaigns for individuals aged 12 months and older unless bridging studies confirm the suitability of MenAfriVac 5 µg for older age groups. 10. The need for a booster dose of the meningococcal A vaccine has not yet been established. 11. Data on co-administration of meningococcal A vaccine with other vaccines, such as diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, oral polio, yellow fever, measles, and rubella vaccines, indicate acceptable safety and efficacy. 12. WHO recommends that all children, including those who are HIV-positive, be immunized against pertussis using either whole-cell pertussis (wP) or acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines. 13. While wP vaccines are associated with higher rates of local and systemic reactogenicity, both wP and aP vaccines have excellent safety profiles. 14. Switching from wP to aP vaccines for primary immunization should only be considered if additional periodic booster doses or maternal immunization can be assured and sustained. 15. National programs currently using wP vaccines should continue their use for primary vaccination, while those using aP vaccines should evaluate the need for additional booster doses and maternal immunization strategies in case of pertussis resurgence. 16. WHO recommends a three-dose primary pertussis vaccination series, starting as early as 6 weeks of age, with subsequent doses given 4–8 weeks apart, ideally completing the series by 6 months of age. 17. For children who have not completed the primary series, vaccination can be administered later than 6 months of age at the earliest opportunity. 18. Countries using alternate primary vaccination schedules with adequate surveillance should continue their schedules while monitoring disease trends. 19. For countries using wP vaccines, the primary series should provide protection for at least 6 years, while protection with aP vaccines may decline before 6 years of age. 20. Only aP-containing vaccines should be used for individuals aged 7 years and older. 21. WHO prioritizes the inclusion of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) in childhood immunization programs, especially in countries with under-5 mortality rates exceeding 50 per 1,000 live births. 22. For infants, WHO recommends either a three-dose primary series (3p+0 schedule) or two primary doses plus a booster (2p+1 schedule), starting as early as 6 weeks of age. 23. WHO recommends that all children worldwide be fully vaccinated against polio, with countries maintaining high coverage levels to support global eradication efforts. 24. WHO no longer recommends an oral polio vaccine (OPV)-only schedule. Countries using OPV-only schedules should add at least one dose of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). 25. In polio-endemic countries or those at high risk of importation, WHO recommends a bivalent OPV (bOPV) birth dose followed by a primary series of three bOPV doses and at least one IPV dose. 26. The primary polio vaccination series can begin at 6 weeks of age, with a minimum interval of 4 weeks between bOPV doses. 27. If only one IPV dose is used, it should be administered at 14 weeks of age or later, when maternal antibodies have waned, and can be co-administered with a bOPV dose. 28. Both OPV and IPV can be safely co-administered with other infant vaccines. 29. For infants starting routine immunization late (after 3 months of age), the IPV dose should be given at the first immunization contact along with bOPV and other recommended vaccines. 30. WHO recommends that endemic countries and those at high risk of wild poliovirus importation should not switch to an IPV-only or sequential IPV-bOPV schedule at this time. 31. Sequential IPV-bOPV schedules or IPV-only schedules may be considered to minimize the risk of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) but only after thorough review of local epidemiology. 32. Polio vaccines (IPV or bOPV) can be safely administered to asymptomatic HIV-infected infants, and HIV testing is not a prerequisite for vaccination. However, bOPV is contraindicated in severely immunocompromised patients, who can safely receive IPV. 33. Rotavirus vaccines (RV1 and RV5) should be administered orally in a two-dose or three-dose schedule, respectively, at the time of DTP1, DTP2, and DTP3 contacts, with at least four weeks between doses. 34. Rotavirus vaccination should be given alongside DTP vaccines regardless of the timing of vaccination. 35. Rotavirus vaccination of healthy children over 2 years of age is not considered necessary. 36. Rubella-containing vaccines are typically administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly at 12–15 months of age but can also be given to children aged 9–11 months and older individuals. 37. Although one dose of rubella vaccine likely provides lifelong protection, most countries using measles-rubella or measles-mumps-rubella vaccines offer a second dose at 15–18 months or 4–6 years for additional protection against measles and mumps. 38. WHO recommends a three-dose primary tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) series, starting as early as 6 weeks of age, with subsequent doses given at least 4 weeks apart and ideally completed by 6 months of age. 39. WHO advises that three TTCV booster doses be provided at 12–23 months, 4–7 years, and 9–15 years of age, with at least 4 years between booster doses. 40. Typhoid vaccination is recommended for school-age and preschool-age children in areas where typhoid fever is a significant public health problem, particularly where antibiotic-resistant Salmonella Typhi is prevalent. 41. The choice of delivery strategy (schoolor community-based) and vaccine type (Vi or Ty21a) should be based on local factors such as age-specific incidence, risk subgroups, and school enrollment rates. 42. Typhoid vaccination is also recommended for outbreak control due to its effectiveness in interrupting outbreaks. 43. Endemic countries should introduce yellow fever vaccine into routine immunization programs, administering it to children at 9–12 months of age alongside the measles vaccine. 44. Pre-exposure prophylaxis for rabies is recommended for individuals at continuous, frequent, or increased risk of exposure due to residence, travel, or occupation. 45. Post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies depends on the type of contact with the suspected rabid animal: no prophylaxis for category I exposures, immediate vaccination for category II, and immediate vaccination with rabies immunoglobulin for category III. 46. HIV-exposed infants and children should receive all vaccines under routine immunization schedules, with inactivated vaccines being safer and more effective for those on antiretroviral therapy or without immunosuppression. 47. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for all infants from birth until 6 months of age, with mothers receiving counseling and support at every postnatal contact. 48. Breastfeeding progress should be assessed at each postnatal contact. 49. Facilities providing maternity services should implement the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding, including policies, staff training, and support for mothers to initiate and maintain breastfeeding. 50. Breast-milk substitutes should only be used in rare cases of maternal or infant conditions where breastfeeding is not possible.
